observations.statement: The paper states its question as the effectiveness of linked regulation and answers it by building and estimating a dynamic moral hazard framework with a regulator, then simulating counterfactual inspection allocations; the descriptive regressions are explicitly framed as suggestive, not causal.

After the descriptive deterrence regressions the authors state that a causal relationship cannot be ascertained because violations are only observed when inspected, expectations drive actions and inspections are targeted on scores; this motivates the structural model.
observations.quote: we cannot ascertain a causal relationship from this analysis

observations.statement: Modelling assumptions are collected in dedicated 'Discussion of assumptions' subsections for both the firm's problem and the regulator's problem, each assumption paired with an institutional justification and a pointer to an appendix robustness test.

The curse of dimensionality is handled by a named assumption (continuation value sufficiency) attributed to an analogous assumption in prior literature; the reduced state space and AR(1) belief transitions are stated in the main text with the formal derivation deferred to the online appendix.

Identification of the second-stage parameters is exposited informally through a simplified one-period, single-plant version of the firm's problem, whose closed-form solution is used to motivate the choice of moments; a variance decomposition of detected violations is used to motivate the moments for the type variances.

Regulator social harm parameters are identified from the regulator's first-order conditions across sectors; the authors note that a binding budget constraint means only relative harms are identified and normalise one sector's harm.

Data are described as an unbalanced panel of the universe of plants regulated by the Texas regulator under two federal acts over a stated multi-year window, aggregated to the plant-year level; plants and firms are defined by the regulator's site and owner identifiers.

The small share of inspections conducted by the federal EPA rather than the state regulator is retained in the sample with a stated rationale, and an online appendix section is cited showing the choice has minimal effect on descriptive, estimation and counterfactual results.
The panel year is defined to start on the date scores are updated rather than the calendar year, stated in a footnote.

Sample sizes are reported per column in the descriptive regression tables and per variable in the summary statistics table; the deterrence table shows N changing with the fixed-effect structure and the inspected-only restriction.
Plant and firm scores are transformed with log(1+x) because of a long right tail; the authors explain that zero corresponds to a clean compliance history.

The outcome for the deterrence regressions is the count of violations uncovered at a plant, and the key regressor is the predicted inspection probability from the first inspection logit specification.

The firm score is defined by an explicit formula (a complexity-point weighted average of plant scores), and the regulator's exact plant-score algorithm is reproduced in the online appendix rather than in the main text.
Violations are mapped to a pollution index used as an alternative welfare measure; the construction steps and alternative constructions are placed in the online appendix.
The number of violations per inspection is used as a proxy for the gravity of bad management, justified by an appendix table showing penalties scale approximately linearly in detected violations.

Observable plant heterogeneity is proxied by six NAICS-based sectors; unobserved heterogeneity is modelled as private types within sector; alternative observables (region, environmental justice index) are tested for relevance in the inspection regressions before being dropped from the model.

The inspection-probability table reports three logit columns with fixed effects listed as Yes/No rows, N and log-likelihood per column; controls (environmental justice index, region FE) are added progressively and the parsimonious column is chosen as the policy function.

The deterrence table lists year FE and a 'Unit FEs' row naming category and firm FE versus plant FE, plus an 'Only Inspected' row for the sample restriction; the text walks through why each column change is made (sorting versus detection).
The structural estimates table reports parameter estimates with standard errors and a note describing how they are computed and the normalisation applied.
The descriptive tables report standard errors in parentheses but the text and table notes do not state the standard error type or clustering level for the logit and deterrence regressions.
Standard errors for the structural parameters are obtained by a bootstrap that resamples with replacement at the firm level, with the number of iterations stated in the table note.
observations.quote: sampling with replacement at the firm level

observations.statement: Model fit is assessed by a table listing each estimation moment with its simulated and empirical value, followed by a binscatter of estimated plant types against the leave-one-out mean of co-owned plants' types.
First-stage (offline) estimates are relegated to an online appendix table while second- and third-stage estimates appear in the main text.
An appendix table is cited to support a modelling assumption (increasing differences) by showing that high-violation plants are more responsive to inspection probability.

Two behavioural threats (strategic avoidance and production reallocation) are tested in the online appendix; the avoidance test exploits firms with plants in multiple regulator regions and the local sourcing of inspectors.

The counterfactual section has a dedicated robustness subsection that summarises appendix checks in prose: within-industry type correlation, regulator internalising compliance costs, longer score histories via AR(1) persistence, and random crackdowns.
Robustness to the regulator's objective is provided by re-expressing counterfactual gains with a pollution-index measure in the main table and by disaggregated sector results in the appendix.
Robustness of the binscatter correlation to controls for observable plant characteristics is placed in an appendix table.
Counterfactual results are reported separately for multi-plant firms, single-plant firms and all firms, with the single-plant rows used to rule out reallocation of enforcement across firm types.
Targeting heterogeneity is shown by a LOWESS-smoothed plot of the change in inspection probability across plant-type quantiles.

Mechanisms are separated by a numerical decomposition: one channel is isolated by holding the score-to-action policy fixed and re-simulating the stationary distribution, the remainder is attributed to the second channel; a stylised two-period model in the appendix justifies additivity.

Before the model, three descriptive facts are presented in sequence (within-firm correlation of violations, targeting on scores, deterrence conditional on plant FE) to motivate the model's ingredients.

Because social costs are identified only up to scale, counterfactual effectiveness is reported as percentage changes relative to an untargeted budget increase; the table note reports the baseline mean violations per plant as a reference.

Descriptive coefficients are translated into implied inspection probabilities and deterrence effects for a 'clean' versus 'bad' plant by chaining the logit and deterrence regressions, and plotted in a figure.
Unlinked-regulation counterfactual results are explicitly benchmarked against the closest prior structural paper.

The commitment assumption is flagged as maintained throughout; the authors state that characterising self-enforcing policies is outside scope and use the mechanism decomposition to argue which channel survives without commitment.
Compliance costs are unobserved, so the correlation in actions is acknowledged to attenuate the correlation in costs under the deterrence regime.
The authors note that ruling out production shifting makes their linked-regulation conclusions conservative, in a footnote.

External validity is argued through the mechanism decomposition: which channel dominates is said to determine how the policy would fare in settings with or without regulator commitment or cross-state ownership.
A summary statistics table reports N, mean, standard deviation and the 1st and 99th percentiles for key variables.
Binscatters with confidence bands are used for raw correlations; regression tables show standard errors in parentheses without significance stars.
The model timing is summarised in a numbered timeline and a timing diagram figure.
Online appendix tables are referenced with an A- prefix and appendix sections by number throughout the main text.
Key equations are annotated with under-braces labelling each economic component (flow benefit, inspection, expected penalty, continuation values).

The introduction previews the counterfactual findings, the mechanism decomposition and additional counterfactuals, then has a numbered contributions subsection and a related-literature subsection; no explicit roadmap paragraph.
Institutional context precedes data, and the context section is organised as short definitional subsections (what is a plant, a firm, an inspection, a violation) before the scoring rules.

Order is context, data, descriptive analysis, model, estimation and identification, results and fit, counterfactuals, then a robustness subsection; robustness appears in a separate subsection at the end of both descriptive and counterfactual sections.
The main text repeatedly defers derivations, algorithms, calibration details, decomposition implementation and most robustness to numbered online appendix sections.
A Data Availability paragraph states that data and code are on Zenodo with a DOI.
No software or package is named in the main text for estimation or regressions.

Data come from the state environmental regulator's administrative records (identifiers, scores, inspections, violations, penalties) combined with an EPA environmental justice index; no access restrictions are mentioned.

Several model parameters are calibrated directly from the regulator's published rules (penalty escalations, score decay), and the discount factor is fixed; a footnote quotes the administrative code decay rule.

Estimation is laid out as three explicit steps (offline calibration, simulated method of moments for firms with nested inner and outer loops, analytic inversion of regulator first-order conditions) with each step's parameters named.
